title: Redwood Discovery - Model selection - Lumen Finance
summary: Intro discovery focused on model selection for mixed workload: multilingual customer support, long-form document summarization, and secure tool-calling for transactions. Discussed context window needs (32k+), open-model tradeoffs, hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments, and next steps for benchmarks, pricing, and security docs.
topics: Model selection: open models (Llama, Mistral, Falcon, Mixtral, Gemma)
Tool/function calling and secure transaction integrations
Performance/latency vs cost tradeoffs and quantization
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-15
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 min (approx)
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Nguyen (Redwood SE), John Becker (CTO - Lumen), Priya Shah (ML Eng), Marcus Lee (Head of Product), Ana Torres (Security)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, and Carlos is our SE, he'll jump into the technical bits. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] John: Yeah hi, thanks. Busy but good. We'll keep this focused — main goal is to pick the right model surface for our production workloads.
[00:12] Maya: Great. Quick agenda: understand your workloads, constraints (latency, cost, security), context window needs, and then we can talk recommended models and deployment modes — hosted/dedicated/private.
[00:20] John: Sounds good. Priya, you want to give a quick run-down of the workloads?
[00:23] Priya: Sure. We have three primary flows: 1) multilingual customer support chat — English, Spanish, French mostly, sometimes Portuguese; 2) long-form doc ingestion and summarization for regulatory filings — those docs can be pretty long, like tens of thousands of words; 3) transaction orchestration where the model needs to call internal APIs to fetch account balances and create holds — so tool-calling with secure credentials is critical. Latency target for chat is 300-600ms p50 ideally, cost needs to be predictable.
[00:50] Marcus: Also to add, we'll have peaks during month-end, and we want predictable throughput more than absolute lowest cost — outages are expensive.
[00:58] Carlos: Super helpful. On the long docs, can you quantify typical document length in tokens or pages?
[01:03] Priya: Most are 30-50 pages, but with appendices can go up to 150 pages. We haven't converted to tokens yet but estimate wanting at least a 32k token window to avoid heavy chunking. For some legal scans, bigger might be nice.
[01:15] Ana: From security side we need SOC2 compliance, customer-controlled KMS for keys, audit logs, SSO/SAML, and data residency for EU users. On-prem may be considered for some regulated accounts.
[01:25] Maya: Good constraints. For model selection, you're skewed towards open models? Priya: Yes, preference for open models for cost and control, but we want parity on quality and function-calling.
[01:35] Carlos: Ok, high-level tradeoffs: open models vary in size, context length, and available optimized builds. Llama 2 70B has 32k variants, Mixtral and Mistral families have different strengths — Mistral generally good few-shot and instruction tuning, Mixtral 8x is peppy for generation. Falcon variants can be strong on certain tasks but may vary on multilingual quality. There's also Gemma from Meta — we've seen good long-context profiles experimentally.
[01:55] Priya: Any clear winners for multilingual? Spanish and French must be first-class citizens.
[01:58] Carlos: Llama 2 and Gemma tend to be strong across Romance languages. Mistral can be good but sometimes less consistent on non-English. We can run language-specific tests. Also tokenization differences matter — a model with more efficient tokenization for Spanish will be cheaper.
[02:15] John: What about context lengths beyond 32k? We might need 64k for some flows.
[02:19] Carlos: We support model variants and some models have 64k or 128k context windows, but there are tradeoffs — CPU/GPU memory and latency increase. Redwood's runtime can do KV-prefetching and streaming to reduce memory footprint; prefix/KV caching helps for repeated context.
[02:33] Maya: For hosted vs dedicated vs private — quick primer: hosted is fastest to get going and cost-efficient for lower commitment. Dedicated gives predictable throughput with reserved GPU pools; Private (VPC/on-prem) is for strict compliance and data residency, with customer-managed networking and KMS.
[02:49] Ana: For regulated customers, private is required. We want to understand migration effort and whether function-calling still works in private.
[02:56] Carlos: Function-calling (tool calling) is supported across all modes. In Private we run the inference plane in your VPC and we integrate with your KMS/HSM for keys. There is some setup (networking, certs) but our engineers run a handoff. We'll share runbook.
[03:10] Priya: How about latency for dedicated clusters — can we hit the 300-600ms target?
[03:14] Carlos: For smaller models (7B-40B) you can often hit that at p50 with dedicated GPUs and optimized kernels. Larger models increase per-token latency. Redwood supports batching and continuous batching can improve throughput while keeping tail latency reasonable. We can tune autoscaling and burst pools for spikes.
[03:28] John: Cost — any rough delta between hosted and dedicated for heavy traffic?
[03:31] Maya: Hosted is usage-based; if you're heavy steady traffic, dedicated reserved capacity often reduces unit cost and gives SLOs. We can model your traffic and show break-even points.
[03:40] Marcus: Tool-calling security — when the model calls internal APIs, we need to limit scope and ensure no secrets leak. How do you handle that?
[03:46] Carlos: We recommend a proxy/adapter pattern: Redwood calls a minimal shim in your VPC that holds secrets and enforces RBAC. We also provide per-request audit logs and token-level tracing in the Console. We'll share our architecture diagram.
[03:58] Ana: Audit logs retention — can we push to our SIEM?
[04:01] Carlos: Yes, logs can stream to your logging endpoint; we also support S3/GCS delivery. Retention and export policies are configurable.
[04:07] Priya: Back to models — how do you recommend testing alternatives?
[04:10] Carlos: Best practice is to pick 2-3 candidate models: one smaller (cost-efficient), one medium (balance), one large (quality/long-context). Run a benchmark using representative prompts (multilingual, long-doc summaries, tool-calls). We'll run throughput/latency/cost projections and QA the outputs against your eval sets.
[04:26] John: Can Redwood host private quantized builds? We want lower memory and cost but keep quality.
[04:30] Maya: Yes, we support quantized variants and can recommend quantization profiles per workload. We also provide guidance on performance regressions and can rollback model variants.
[04:37] Marcus: Any gotchas with tokenization when comparing models?
[04:40] Carlos: Absolutely — different tokenizers change token counts for same input, affecting cost and context usage. We'll include tokenization probes in the benchmark.
[04:47] Priya: How long do pilots usually take? We have tight Q4 timelines.
[04:50] Maya: For a focused pilot (benchmarks + 2-week integration) typically 4–6 weeks end-to-end. For Private/on-prem it can take longer due to network approvals, but we have enterprise onboarding sprints.
[04:59] John: Competitors — we're also talking to OpenAI for hosted API and Anthropic; important to see cost/quality tradeoffs.
[05:05] Maya: Understood. We'll make sure the benchmark compares to those baselines where possible.
[05:09] Carlos: Quick note — if you need extreme long-context (100k+), we can explore Hybrid approaches: chunking + retrieval + local RAG to avoid loading entire doc into context. That often works better than huge context windows.
[05:22] Ana: Security doc request — we'll need SOC2, ISO certs, data flow diagrams, and encryption details.
[05:27] Maya: We'll send the security package and our SOC2 reports after the call.
[05:31] John: Great. Next steps?
[05:33] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send pricing spreadsheet and security docs, run an initial benchmark against 3 models (we propose Llama-2-70B-32k, Mixtral-ish 8x and a Falcon/Gemma 32k variant), include tokenization probes and multilingual tests. Then schedule a follow-up demo to walk through benchmark results and recommended deployment mode.
[05:53] Priya: That works. Also we'd like a short doc on recommended approach for tool-calling security architecture.
[05:58] Maya: Noted. Carlos, anything else?
[06:00] Carlos: I'll include a sample prompt set and details on KV caching and batching knobs we'll sweep in the benchmark. Also will outline how function-calling integrates in Private mode.
[06:09] John: Okay, thanks.
[06:11] Maya: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links and schedule the benchmark kickoff.
[06:16] End of recording.

Notes on transcription quality: some model names may be mis-transcribed (e.g., "Llama" -> "Lama", "Mistral" -> "Mister all"), and technical terms like KV cache sometimes appear as "K V cash".
